About: E = −dV/dr

Source

Topic
Electrostatic potential and field — their exact relation.
Concept
The electric field is minus the gradient of the potential: where equipotentials crowd, the field is strong.
Serves
Reading a contour map for field strength and direction; the practical meaning of "gradient".
Misconception
Treating V and E as independent quantities computed by separate formulas.

Guided Inquiry

1 · Predict

The probe ★ moves outward, from close to the charge to far away. How do the steepness of V(r) and the field strength E change?

2 · Observe

Drag the probe ★ on the left panel. Watch the tangent line on the right — its slope IS the gradient dV/dr. Notice that the two readouts E and −dV/dr agree to four decimal places at every position, every charge.

Move the probe close: contours crowd, V(r) plunges, tangent line stands up steep, both numbers climb together. Move it far: contours space out, V(r) flattens, tangent line lies almost flat, both numbers shrink together.

3 · Verify

E and −dV/dr both change as you move the probe. What value does their ratio (−dV/dr)/E hold?

4 · Resolve

The map contains the field. A contour map of V is not a separate diagram from a field map — it IS the field map. Where the contours crowd, V changes rapidly with distance; that rate of change, negated, is E.

The units differ (V vs V/m) precisely because one is the rate of change of the other with distance. Explore freely: change q, drag the probe anywhere, and confirm — the two numbers are always equal.

01

At a glance

A point charge makes a potential V around it. The sim shows V twice: as rings on a map, and as a curve against the distance r. A probe star slides along both, and the sim reads out the field E at the probe.

What you'll learn

  • What a contour map of the potential shows.
  • How the field E and the potential V are connected.
  • What the slope of the V(r) curve means.
  • How to read field strength from the spacing of the rings.
The probe sits on a ring. Every point on that ring has the same potential.

What's on screen

  • The charge and the rings around it, each labelled with its V.
  • The probe ★ on the dashed line, and a red arrow marked E.
  • The V(r) plot: the blue curve, and an amber tangent line at the probe.
  • Readouts for E, the tangent's slope, and a ratio.
See itLook at the scene as it opens. Watch for: rings around a pink + charge, a star on the dashed line, and a star and an amber line on the blue curve.

03

A point charge sets the potential V = q/r around it

The potential V at a point is the work per unit charge to bring a test charge there from far away. For a point charge, with k = 1:

V(r) = q / r
V is positive for q > 0 and negative for q < 0. It has no direction.
  • V depends only on the distance r, so every ring around the charge has one constant V. Such a ring is an equipotential: r = q/V.
  • The map draws a ring at every step of 0.5 in V and labels it where there is room.
  • The blue curve on the plot is the same V(r) along the dashed line.
  • Doubling q doubles V at every r, so a ring of the old V moves out to twice its radius.
See itRaise q from +1.00 to +2.00. Watch for: twice as many rings, and the star on the plot rising from V = 1 to V = 2 at the same r.
04

The field is minus the slope of the potential

The field of a point charge is E = q/r², pointing away from a positive charge. Differentiate the potential and the same thing comes out:

E = −dV/dr = −d(q/r)/dr = q / r²
The amber tangent line on the plot has slope dV/dr. Its negative is E.
q = +1.00V = q/rslope dV/drE
r = 0.502.000−4.0004.000
r = 1.001.000−1.0001.000
r = 2.000.500−0.2500.250

Going outward, the curve flattens and E weakens together. They are one quantity: a steep V means a strong E. The minus sign says E points toward falling V, and V falls as you move away from a positive charge.

See itSlide the probe in from r = 2.00 to 0.50. Watch for: the tangent steepening, and E rising from 0.2500 to 4.0000 with the slope readout.
05

The two readouts agree at every distance and charge

The sim finds the slope of V(r) numerically, from two nearby points. It finds E from the formula q/r². These are separate calculations, yet they match to four decimal places, so their ratio reads 1.0000 everywhere.

  • At q = +2.00 and r = 1.00 both readouts show 2.0000.
  • At q = +1.00 and r = 0.30 both show 11.1111.
  • For a negative charge V is negative and the curve rises toward zero as r grows. Its slope is positive, so −dV/dr is negative. E is negative as well, and the red arrow points inward.
  • At q = 0 there is no field and no slope. The ratio would be 0/0, so the sim shows a dash instead.

The ratio is 1 because E is defined as the minus gradient of V. It tests the algebra above, not a new law.

See itSet q to −2.00 at r = 1.00. Watch for: the arrow turning inward, E and the slope readout both showing −2.0000, and the ratio 1.0000.
06

Where the rings crowd, the field is strong

The rings are spaced at equal steps of ΔV = 0.5. Between two neighbouring rings the average slope is ΔV/Δr, which is close to E there. So a small gap Δr means a large E:

|E| ≈ ΔV / Δr
The contour map is a field map, once you read the spacing.
q = +1.00, rings atgap ΔrΔV/ΔrE at the two rings
r = 2.00 and 1.001.0000.500.25 and 1.00
r = 1.00 and 0.6670.3331.501.00 and 2.25

Rings crowd near the charge, where E grows as 1/r². Raising q packs more rings into the same space, because a larger q means a larger E at the same r.

See itAt r = 1.00, raise q from +1.00 to +3.00. Watch for: the rings packing in around the charge, and E rising to 3.0000.
07

Where it matters

  • In three dimensions. The sim has only a radial line. In general E = −∇V: the field points the way V falls fastest, and it is perpendicular to the equipotential through that point.
  • Uniform field. Between parallel plates V changes at a steady rate, so E = −ΔV/Δx is the same everywhere, and the equipotentials are equally spaced planes.
  • Units. E is a volt per metre, and 1 V/m equals 1 N/C. This is why a potential is quoted in V and a field in V/m.
  • Careful. E depends on the slope of V, not its value. A place where V = 0 can still have a strong field, and where V is constant, E = 0.
08

Summary

In one line. The potential of a point charge falls with distance. The sim lets you see how its slope on the plot and the field at the probe are linked.

Key points

  • V = q/r, and E = −dV/dr = q/r².
  • The tangent's slope on the V(r) plot is −E. A steep V means a strong E.
  • The ratio (−dV/dr)/E is 1 at every r and every q ≠ 0.
  • Rings at equal ΔV crowd where E is large: |E| ≈ ΔV/Δr.

Common mix-ups

  • "V and E come from separate formulas." E is the minus slope of V.
  • "A large V means a large E." E follows the slope, not the height. With q = 1, V is 2 and E is 4 at r = 0.50, but V is 0.5 and E is only 0.25 at r = 2.00.
  • "The field points toward higher V." It points toward lower V.

Things to try on your own

  • Set q = 0.5 and find the r where E drops to 0.10.
  • Find the largest r at which a ring is drawn for q = +1.00.
  • Predict E at r = 0.40 with q = +2.00, then check it.
